units.title: Asymptotic Analysis & Linear Structures
units.description: Big-O, Omega, Theta notation, amortized analysis, linked lists, stacks, queues, and skip lists.

topics.title: Asymptotic Notations & Master Theorem
topics.content:
Asymptotic analysis describes the limiting behavior of execution time or memory when input size $n$ approaches infinity.

### Big-O ($O$), Big-$\Omega$, Big-$\Theta$
- **$O(g(n))$**: Upper bound. $f(n) \le c \cdot g(n)$ for all $n \ge n_0$.
- **$\Omega(g(n))$**: Lower bound. $f(n) \ge c \cdot g(n)$ for all $n \ge n_0$.
- **$\Theta(g(n))$**: Tight bound. $c_1 g(n) \le f(n) \le c_2 g(n)$.

### Master Theorem
For recurrences of the form $T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n)$ where $a \ge 1, b > 1$:
- If $f(n) = O(n^{\log_b a - \epsilon})$, then $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a})$.
- If $f(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log^k n)$, then $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log^{k+1} n)$.
- If $f(n) = \Omega(n^{\log_b a + \epsilon})$ and regularity condition holds, $T(n) = \Theta(f(n))$.
keyPoints: Big-O represents the worst-case asymptotic upper bound.
Master theorem solves divide-and-conquer recurrences directly, without expanding the recursion tree.
Amortized analysis averages cost across a sequence of operations.

topics.title: Singly & Doubly Linked Lists with Cycle Detection
topics.content:
Linked lists represent linear sequences of nodes containing data and reference pointers.

Floyd's Cycle Finding Algorithm (Tortoise and Hare) uses two pointers moving at different speeds (1 step and 2 steps). If a cycle exists, they are guaranteed to meet inside the loop in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ auxiliary space.
keyPoints: Insertions at head take $O(1)$ time.
Floyd’s algorithm detects cycles without extra hash table storage.
Doubly linked lists enable $O(1)$ deletion when the node pointer is known.

units.title: Non-Linear Structures: Trees & Heaps
units.description: Binary search trees, AVL self-balancing trees, Red-Black properties, and priority queues.

topics.title: AVL Trees & Rotations
topics.content:
An AVL tree is a self-balancing binary search tree where the heights of the two child subtrees of any node differ by at most 1.

Balance Factor: $BF = \text{height}(left) - \text{height}(right) \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$.

When an insertion unbalances a node, four rotation cases restore balance in $O(1)$ time: Left-Left (Single Right Rotation), Right-Right (Single Left Rotation), Left-Right (Double Rotation), and Right-Left (Double Rotation).
keyPoints: Guarantees $O(\log n)$ search, insertion, and deletion.
More rigidly balanced than Red-Black trees, making lookups faster.

subjects.name: Operating Systems
subjects.description: Process management, concurrency, CPU scheduling algorithms, virtual memory paging, and file systems.

units.title: Processes, Threads & CPU Scheduling
units.description: Process Control Block (PCB), context switching, POSIX threads, and scheduling heuristics.

topics.title: Process Lifecycle & Context Switching
topics.content:
A process is an instance of an executing program consisting of text segment, data segment, heap, and call stack.

State Diagram: New -> Ready -> Running -> Waiting (Blocked) -> Terminated.

Context switching saves the CPU register state into the PCB of the current process and reloads the PCB of the next scheduled process. This incurs CPU overhead without executing user instructions.
keyPoints: PCB stores Program Counter, Registers, Memory Limits, Open File Descriptors.
Context switch overhead is influenced by cache pollution and TLB flushes.

topics.title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms: Round Robin & SRTF
topics.content:
Schedulers optimize turnaround time, waiting time, and response time.

- **Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)**: Preemptive version of SJF; mathematically minimizes average waiting time, but risks starvation of long jobs.
- **Round Robin (RR)**: Time quantum $q$ slices CPU fairly among ready processes. If $q$ is too small, context switch overhead dominates; if too large, it degrades to FCFS.
keyPoints: SRTF gives minimal average waiting time.
Round Robin prevents starvation with bounded latency.

units.title: Synchronization & Deadlocks
units.description: Critical section problem, semaphores, mutexes, monitors, and Banker's algorithm.

topics.title: Semaphores & Dining Philosophers Problem
topics.content:
A semaphore is an integer variable accessed via atomic `wait()` (P) and `signal()` (V) operations.

Deadlock requires four simultaneous Coffman conditions:
1. Mutual Exclusion
2. Hold and Wait
3. No Preemption
4. Circular Wait

Dining Philosophers can be solved deadlock-free by resource hierarchy (odd/even ordering) or an asymmetric pickup strategy.
keyPoints: Counting vs Binary semaphores.
Banker’s algorithm tests safe states before granting resource requests.

units.title: Relational Model & Normalization
units.description: Functional dependencies, lossless join decomposition, and 3NF vs BCNF.

topics.title: Functional Dependencies & BCNF Normalization
topics.content:
Normalization eliminates insertion, update, and deletion anomalies while minimizing redundancy.

- **1NF**: Atomic attribute values.
- **2NF**: In 1NF and no non-prime attribute is partially dependent on any candidate key.
- **3NF**: In 2NF and no transitive dependencies ($X \to Y \implies X$ is superkey or $Y$ is prime).
- **Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)**: For every non-trivial functional dependency $X \to Y$, $X$ MUST be a superkey.
keyPoints: BCNF eliminates all redundancy based on functional dependencies.
3NF guarantees dependency preservation; BCNF may lose dependencies during decomposition.

units.title: Transactions & Concurrency Control
units.description: ACID properties, serializability, two-phase locking (2PL), and WAL logging.

topics.title: ACID Properties & Two-Phase Locking (2PL)
topics.content:
Transactions must satisfy ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability.

**Two-Phase Locking (2PL)** ensures conflict serializability by dividing locking into:
1. Growing Phase: Locks acquired, no locks released.
2. Shrinking Phase: Locks released, no new locks acquired.

**Strict 2PL** holds all exclusive locks until transaction commit/abort, preventing cascading rollbacks.
keyPoints: 2PL guarantees conflict serializability.
Strict 2PL prevents dirty reads and cascading rollbacks.

units.title: Transport Layer & Congestion Control
units.description: TCP 3-way handshake, sequence numbers, flow control, Reno/Cubic algorithms.

topics.title: TCP 3-Way Handshake & Reliable Delivery
topics.content:
TCP provides connection-oriented, ordered, reliable byte-stream transmission.

Handshake sequence:
1. Client sends `SYN` (seq = x)
2. Server replies `SYN-ACK` (seq = y, ack = x + 1)
3. Client responds `ACK` (seq = x + 1, ack = y + 1)

Congestion control phases: Slow Start (exponential window growth), Congestion Avoidance (additive increase), and Fast Retransmit / Fast Recovery upon receiving 3 duplicate ACKs.
keyPoints: SYN-ACK exchange establishes synchronized initial sequence numbers (ISNs).
Additive Increase Multiplicative Decrease (AIMD) guarantees fairness across competing flows.

units.title: Graph Theory & Eulerian/Hamiltonian Paths
units.description: Adjacency matrices, Euler circuits, Dirac theorem, planar graphs, and chromatic numbers.

topics.title: Eulerian Graphs & Fleury’s Algorithm
topics.content:
A connected graph contains an **Eulerian circuit** (traversing every edge exactly once and returning to start) if and only if every vertex has an **even degree**.

A graph has an Eulerian path if exactly 0 or 2 vertices have an odd degree.
keyPoints: Eulerian circuits depend solely on vertex degrees.
Hamiltonian paths (visiting every vertex once) are NP-complete in general.

topics.title: A* Search Algorithm & Admissible Heuristics
topics.content:
A* evaluates nodes using evaluation function $f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$:
- $g(n)$: Exact path cost from start to node $n$.
- $h(n)$: Estimated heuristic cost from $n$ to goal.

**Admissibility**: An admissible heuristic never overestimates the true remaining distance ($h(n) \le h^*(n)$). Admissible heuristics guarantee optimality in tree search, while consistency (monotonicity) guarantees optimality in graph search without reopening closed nodes.
keyPoints: A* is both complete and optimal under an admissible heuristic.
Manhattan distance is admissible for grid pathfinding with 4-directional moves.

notes.title: Operating Systems: Semaphores & Deadlock Coffman Conditions
notes.subject: Operating Systems
notes.content:
# Operating Systems: Concurrency & Deadlocks

## Critical Section Problem
A critical section is a piece of code that accesses shared resources. A valid synchronization solution must satisfy:
1. **Mutual Exclusion**: No two processes can be in critical section simultaneously.
2. **Progress**: Selection cannot be postponed indefinitely if no one is in critical section.
3. **Bounded Waiting**: Bound on how many times others can enter before a request is granted.

## Semaphores
A semaphore $S$ is an integer accessed through two atomic primitives:
```c
void wait(Semaphore S) {
    while (S <= 0); // busy wait or block
    S--;
}

void signal(Semaphore S) {
    S++;
}
```

## Four Coffman Conditions for Deadlock
1. **Mutual Exclusion**: At least one resource held in non-shareable mode.
2. **Hold and Wait**: Process holds resource while requesting another.
3. **No Preemption**: Resources cannot be forcibly seized.
4. **Circular Wait**: Set of processes {P0, P1, ..., Pn} where P0 waits for P1, Pn waits for P0.
notes.summary: Detailed summary of synchronization requirements (Mutual Exclusion, Progress, Bounded Waiting), atomic semaphore semantics, and the 4 Coffman deadlock conditions.

notes.title: Dynamic Programming: 0/1 Knapsack & Memoization Patterns
notes.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
notes.content:
# Dynamic Programming: 0/1 Knapsack

## Problem Definition
Given $N$ items with weights $W_i$ and values $V_i$, and a knapsack capacity $C$, find the maximum total value such that total weight $\le C$.

## Recurrence Relation
Let $dp[i][w]$ be the max value using a subset of the first $i$ items with capacity $w$:
$$dp[i][w] = \max(dp[i-1][w], \; dp[i-1][w - W_i] + V_i) \quad \text{if } w \ge W_i$$
Otherwise:
$$dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w]$$

## Space Optimization
Since $dp[i]$ only depends on $dp[i-1]$, we can reduce memory to a 1D array of size $C + 1$ by iterating the capacity backwards from $C$ down to $W_i$.
notes.summary: Mathematical formulation of the 0/1 Knapsack problem with 2D state transitions and 1D space optimization technique.

quizzes.explanation: Because an AVL tree strictly enforces that child heights differ by at most 1, its height is strictly bounded by 1.44 log n, giving guaranteed O(log n) search time.

flashcards.subject: Operating Systems
flashcards.front: What is Thrashing in Virtual Memory?
flashcards.back: Thrashing occurs when a computer spends more time paging data in and out of swap space than executing instructions, caused by insufficient physical frames for the active working sets.

flashcards.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
flashcards.front: What is the worst-case time complexity of QuickSort?
flashcards.back: O(n^2), which happens when the pivot chosen is always the extreme (minimum or maximum) element in an already sorted or reverse-sorted array without random pivoting.

flashcards.subject: Database Management Systems
flashcards.front: What does the ACID "Isolation" property mean?
flashcards.back: Transactions execute concurrently without interference; the intermediate states of a transaction are invisible to other concurrent transactions.

flashcards.subject: Computer Networks
flashcards.front: What is the MTU of standard Ethernet?
flashcards.back: 1500 bytes (payload size excluding the Ethernet header and frame check sequence).

flashcards.subject: Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning
flashcards.front: What makes a heuristic admissible in A* search?
flashcards.back: A heuristic h(n) is admissible if it never overestimates the true lowest cost from node n to the goal: h(n) <= h*(n).

pyqs.subject: Operating Systems
pyqs.question: Consider a system with 5 processes (P0-P4) and 3 resource types (A, B, C) with total instances A=10, B=5, C=7. Allocation: P0=(0,1,0), P1=(2,0,0), P2=(3,0,2), P3=(2,1,1), P4=(0,0,2). Max: P0=(7,5,3), P1=(3,2,2), P2=(9,0,2), P3=(2,2,2), P4=(4,3,3). Available = (3,3,2). Explain how the Banker’s Algorithm determines whether the system is in a safe state, and compute the safe sequence.
pyqs.modelAnswer: The Banker’s algorithm simulates resource allocation by checking if there exists an ordering of processes such that each process can satisfy its maximum remaining resource need using currently available resources plus resources freed by terminated processes.
keySteps: Calculate Need Matrix: Need[i][j] = Max[i][j] - Allocation[i][j].
Initialize Work = Available and Finish[i] = false for all i.
Find process Pi where Finish[i] == false and Need[i] <= Work.
Simulate completion: Work = Work + Allocation[i], Finish[i] = true.
If all processes finish, state is SAFE with sequence <P1, P3, P4, P0, P2>.

pyqs.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
pyqs.question: Prove that comparison-based sorting algorithms cannot achieve a worst-case time complexity better than Omega(n log n).
pyqs.modelAnswer: Any comparison sort can be modeled as a decision tree where each internal node represents a comparison A[i] <= A[j] and each leaf represents one of the n! possible permutations of elements.
keySteps: Number of leaves L >= n! to produce all possible sorted permutations.
A binary tree of height h has at most 2^h leaves (L <= 2^h).
Hence 2^h >= n!, which gives h >= log2(n!).
By Stirling’s approximation, log2(n!) = Theta(n log n).
Since height represents comparisons in worst case, worst case is Omega(n log n).
